output.title: Exit plans get expensive when the workflow stays in your head
output.body:
If you are an owner-operator, the cost of an exit plan is not just legal fees or advisor time. It is also the work you have not turned into a repeatable process yet.

In the representative small-business scenario from the brief, that looks like repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads, and manual invoice or data work. That is a persona example, not a customer result. If that load sits with one person, it can crowd out the boring but necessary exit work: documenting the process, handing it over, and deciding what still needs human approval.

That is where a bounded workflow decision helps. Pick one recurring task that is both frequent and repeatable, such as customer-inquiry triage, invoice logging, or lead routing. Ask: which one takes the most time this week, and which one would be easiest to define clearly?

Then make a simple call: if the task is well-bounded, test whether AI fits it before you think about a broader automation push. Bareni’s normal sequence is a free diagnostic, then a one-page pilot proposal, then a paid MVP in days. Those timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

The point is not to automate everything. It is to reduce the manual backlog so the owner can spend time on documentation, succession planning, or buyer conversations while final approval and business authority stay human.

Start by auditing the one task that keeps showing up on your list this week. That is usually the place where the exit plan gets less expensive.
